title: Keep what you loved
hookLine: candles on Friday without certainty, carols without church: keeping a ritual without the whole creed is common, and it isn't fake

cards: Someone who isn't sure what they believe still lights candles on Friday night. Someone who stopped going to church still sings every word of the carols.
Someone who hasn't prayed in years still says a blessing over food, because their grandmother did. Are they doing it wrong? Is it fake to keep a ritual without the whole creed behind it?
Plenty of people quietly wonder. Today: keep what you loved.

teach.h: PRACTICE AND BELIEF DON'T ALWAYS MATCH.
teach.b: First, it's common, and it's old. In many families, practice and belief don't move in step. People keep a holiday, a fast, a song or a meal long after they've stopped being sure about everything behind it.
Some traditions have deep room for this. Jewish life, for instance, has long included secular and cultural Jews, and many lead a seder at home whatever they believe. Second, why rituals help.
Researchers who study ritual find that repeated, structured acts can steady people when life feels out of control, and bind them to each other.
The anthropologist Dimitris Xygalatas has spent years measuring this, in festivals and in homes. A ritual doesn't need you to be certain to do its work. Third, keep it honest.
A ritual belongs to a people. If you keep one from the tradition you grew up in, it's yours too.
If you borrow one from a tradition that isn't yours, do it the way you visited this year: as a guest. Learn what it means. Ask someone who keeps it.
Don't remix it into something it isn't. Fourth, how to choose. Ask of each ritual: what did it give me?
Calm, company, a marked season, a thread back to someone I loved?

teach.h: KEEP THE GIVING, LEAVE THE HURT.
teach.b: Keep the giving. Leave what hurt. Some people find that, kept long enough, an old ritual starts to mean something new.
Some find their way back into the whole tradition through it. Either is fine.

how: Many people keep family rituals, such as holiday candles, songs, a blessing over food or a festival meal, whatever their beliefs; borrowing a ritual from another tradition is done as a guest, by learning its meaning from those who keep it.

o: a superstition with no real effect on anyone
a belief you must hold before you can take part
a repeated act that marks time and binds people

games.q: you stopped believing much of what you grew up with, but you miss lighting the lamp at the festival. what fits this path?
o: never light it again, or it's hypocritical.
light it, knowing what it gives you: calm, a season, a thread to family.
games.why: keep the giving. a ritual can do its work without certainty, and it may come to mean something new.

practice: Bring to mind one ritual from your childhood or your family, a candle, a song, a meal, a word before sleep, the smell of a holiday kitchen, and let it play slowly in your mind.
Notice what it gave you: calm, belonging, a sense of the year turning. Breathe with that, and let everything else sit quietly to one side.

wordCard.voice: Ritual, from the Latin ritus, a rite or custom: a repeated act that marks time and binds people. You can keep one gratefully. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a rite, a custom, especially a religious one; the root of ritual.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the giving. Whatever a ritual gave you, it's allowed to stay. That's day three hundred twenty-seven.
